summary.text: 妈 means “mother” or “mama.” It is the standardized simplified form of 媽, whose visible parts are 女 and 馬: 女 contributes a female-related meaning, while 馬 serves as a phonetic component.

formation.text: The traditional graph 媽 is phonosemantic: 女 contributes a female-related meaning and 馬 supplies a sound cue. In Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese, 馬 *mraːʔ and 媽 *maːʔ share an initial and have broadly similar rhymes, though the vowels differ. The simplified graph 妈 retains 女 and writes 馬 as 马.

components.text: 女 contributes a female-related meaning in 媽 and 妈.
马 is the standardized simplified form of 馬 within 妈. 馬 is analyzed as the phonetic component; the cited older readings are similar enough to support that analysis despite their vowel difference.

sound.text: In Zhengzhang Shangfang Old Chinese, 馬 *mraːʔ and 媽 *maːʔ share an initial and have broadly similar rhymes, though their vowels differ; this supports a probable phonetic relation.
In modern Standard Mandarin, 馬 mǎ and 媽 mā share an initial but differ in tone. This current resemblance does not establish their historical sound relationship.

history.text: The graph 媽 is not recorded in Shuowen, and no earlier paleographic form is established in the cited evidence. The evidence reports that the traditional character has 女 and 馬 as its visible sides; no ancient graphic sequence is established here.
In the standardized simplified graph 妈, 馬 is written as 马.

uncertainties.text: The phonetic analysis has a Zhengzhang Old Chinese comparison, but the cited materials do not provide a matched comparison from another reconstruction system. Modern Mandarin readings alone do not establish the historical sound relationship.

senses.text: The character is cited with the meaning “mother” in 龍龕手鑑; its date and exact wording have not been verified from the primary page.

senses.gloss: form of address for female elders, older women, and servants in northern usage
senses.text: Dictionaries record these forms of address, but do not date them or establish that they developed from the mother sense.
A dictionary excerpt lists an obsolete “mare” sense as a single-attestation use, without a dated citation linking it to the mother sense.

limitations.text: The recorded senses do not establish a dated path among “mother,” the female-address uses, and “mare,” so no development is inferred.
A secondary account relates 媽 to 母 and proposes an older-language source, but the word history and any semantic path are not established here.
